bibliography.abstract: The article examines Constantinos A. Doxiadis and Adriano Olivetti as parallel yet distinct actors in mid-twentieth-century industrial urbanism, arguing that both developed integrated planning models that combined architecture, design, and emerging computational or organizational systems to construct what may be understood as ‘entopian’ or ‘concrete utopian’ settlements. It argues that both figures developed integrated planning models in which architecture, design, industrial production, and computational or organisational systems were mobilized to reconfigure the relationship between work, habitation, and community. It is structured through a comparative analysis of two primary case studies: Adriano Olivetti’s industrial and civic system in Ivrea and Constantinos Doxiadis’ settlement of ‘Aspra Spitia' [‘White Houses’], treating them as interconnected expressions of a broader Mediterranean framework of technocratic humanism, in which industrial modernization is reframed through spatial, social, and organizational design. This comparison is extended through an examination of two computational infrastructures: Olivetti’s Elea 9003 computer and the Doxiadis Associates Computer Center (DACC) in Athens. These are interpreted as early experiments in computational urbanism, where information processing becomes integral to planning, analysis, and governance. The article argues that, despite differences in institutional context and methodological orientation, both approaches converge in their attempt to reconcile industrial production with human-scale urbanism.

bibliography.title: Technocratic humanism and computational urbanism: Adriano Olivetti, Constantinos A. Doxiadis, and industrial settlements in Ivrea and ‘Aspra Spitia’

orgs.label: United States Department of the Interior

en.what: This historical study compares the mid-twentieth-century industrial urbanism models of Adriano Olivetti in Ivrea, Italy, and Constantinos A. Doxiadis in Aspra Spitia, Greece. It analyzes how both figures integrated architecture, social design, and early computational infrastructures—specifically Olivetti's Elea 9003 computer and the Doxiadis Associates Computer Center in Athens—to manage and plan human-scale industrial settlements.
en.why: It traces the historical roots of modern computational urbanism, demonstrating that the integration of information processing, governance, and spatial planning emerged much earlier than the contemporary 'smart city' era as an attempt to balance industrialization with humanistic design.
